\section{Conclusion}
\label{sec:conclusion}

DisPeD's seven controlled Stage~1 variants establish that continued pretraining is the primary mechanism for cross-attack generalization: MLM without labels bridges the dominant $\sim$62\,pp gap (vanilla 0.28 $\to$ MLM 0.91$\pm$0.12), with near-perfect early detection (F1 $\geq$ 0.97 at $K \leq 5$). Any continued pretraining bridges most of this gap; Wikipedia MLM (0.90$\pm$0.12) nearly matches jailbreak-domain MLM at full length, while jailbreak-domain text provides a meaningful advantage for early detection ($K$=2: 8\,pp gap). Classification supervision adds stability (9-class 0.997$\pm$0.006 vs.\ MLM 0.91$\pm$0.12), perturbation robustness with a three-layer attribution (classification structure provides full-length robustness, label granularity adds $K$=2 robustness, correct fine-grained labels add $K$=1 robustness), and interpretability through strategy trajectories. These results reframe multi-turn jailbreak detection as primarily a domain adaptation problem.

\paragraph{Limitations and future work.}
The dataset is small (500 training, 160 OOD test conversations) and synthetically generated by Qwen3-8B, which may not capture the full diversity of real-world attack strategies.
TF-IDF achieves F1 = 0.944 on DD, indicating substantial lexical separability in the current evaluation data; DisPeD's advantage over bag-of-words is strongest under perturbation (0\,pp vs.\ $\sim$12\,pp degradation) and for interpretability via strategy trajectories.
The perturbation robustness evaluation uses $n$=76 paraphrased conversations, where tier boundaries correspond to 1--3 misclassifications; larger-scale evaluation is needed to confirm the three-layer attribution pattern.
Binary and scrambled variants report single-seed results; multi-seed evaluation would strengthen the comparison with 3-seed variants.
Only persuasion-mediated multi-turn attacks fall within scope; single-turn token-level attacks~\citep{zou2023gcg} and non-persuasive multi-turn strategies are not addressed.

Future work should evaluate on human-generated red-teaming conversations, scale to larger multi-source datasets spanning additional attack families, and test robustness against adaptive adversaries who are aware of the domain-specific features that DisPeD relies on.
The finding that continued pretraining is the primary mechanism suggests that scaling training data diversity (more attack families, more generation models) may yield further improvements without architectural changes.

\section{Conclusion}
\label{sec:conclusion}

DisPeD's seven controlled Stage~1 variants establish that continued pretraining is the primary mechanism for cross-attack generalization: MLM without labels bridges the dominant $\sim$62\,pp gap (vanilla 0.28 $\to$ MLM 0.91$\pm$0.12), with near-perfect early detection (F1 $\geq$ 0.97 at $K \leq 5$). Any continued pretraining bridges most of this gap; Wikipedia MLM (0.90$\pm$0.12) nearly matches jailbreak-domain MLM at full length, while jailbreak-domain text provides a meaningful advantage for early detection ($K$=2: 8\,pp gap). Classification supervision adds stability (9-class 0.997$\pm$0.005 vs.\ MLM 0.91$\pm$0.12), perturbation robustness with a three-layer attribution (classification structure provides full-length robustness, label granularity adds $K$=2 robustness, correct fine-grained labels add $K$=1 robustness), and interpretability through strategy trajectories. These results reframe multi-turn jailbreak detection as primarily a domain adaptation problem.

\paragraph{Limitations and future work.}
The dataset is small (500 training, 160 OOD test conversations) and synthetically generated by Qwen3-8B, which may not capture the full diversity of real-world attack strategies.
TF-IDF achieves F1 = 0.944 on DD, indicating substantial lexical separability in the current evaluation data; DisPeD's advantage over bag-of-words is strongest under perturbation (0\,pp vs.\ $\sim$12\,pp degradation) and for interpretability via strategy trajectories.
The perturbation robustness evaluation uses $n$=76 paraphrased conversations, where tier boundaries correspond to 1--3 misclassifications; larger-scale evaluation is needed to confirm the three-layer attribution pattern.
Binary and scrambled variants report single-seed results; multi-seed evaluation would strengthen the comparison with 3-seed variants.
Only persuasion-mediated multi-turn attacks fall within scope; single-turn token-level attacks~\citep{zou2023gcg} and non-persuasive multi-turn strategies are not addressed.

Future work should evaluate on human-generated red-teaming conversations, scale to larger multi-source datasets spanning additional attack families, and test robustness against adaptive adversaries who are aware of the domain-specific features that DisPeD relies on.
The finding that continued pretraining is the primary mechanism suggests that scaling training data diversity (more attack families, more generation models) may yield further improvements without architectural changes.
